key_findings.finding: A primary in-vitro study (PMID 10752932; IOVS 2000) directly tested cholestanol (5alpha-cholestan-3beta-ol/dihydrocholesterol) in cultured corneal endothelial cells and lens epithelial cells. Cells were exposed to 10 microg/mL cholestanol in ethanol in MEM plus 10% fetal bovine serum, with 10 microg/mL cholesterol in ethanol and 1% ethanol as comparators. Cholestanol caused significant loss of viability in both cell types, more TUNEL-positive nuclei and quantitatively increased apoptotic DNA fragmentation in a time-dependent manner, with increased ICE and CPP32/caspase-3 protease activity; the authors concluded that cellular uptake of cholestanol led to apoptosis.

source_tools.relevance: Primary study abstract and extracted methods/results

key_findings.finding: For corneal endothelial cells, the available primary evidence supports direct cholestanol-induced apoptosis under the tested in-vitro conditions. The study used TUNEL/laser cytometry, viability assessment, apoptotic DNA-fragmentation quantification, and ICE/CPP32 activity; however, the accessible record does not provide the exact species/line, exposure duration(s), replicate details, or full dose-response. MeSH indexing includes cattle, suggesting an animal-derived model, but this should not be treated as a fully documented cell-model detail.

For lens epithelial cells, the same primary study supports direct cholestanol-induced apoptosis under the tested in-vitro conditions, based on reduced viability, increased TUNEL staining/apoptotic DNA fragmentation over time, and increased ICE/CPP32 activity. As for corneal endothelium, exact cell source, exposure time points, and dose-response are not available in the accessible abstract.

The study explicitly included cholesterol as a sterol comparator: 10 microg/mL cholesterol did not produce the increased nuclear TUNEL staining seen with 10 microg/mL cholestanol, and 1% ethanol was the vehicle control. Thus, the reported apoptotic effect is not evidence for cholesterol generally; it is specific to cholestanol in this experiment.

source_tools.relevance: Direct sterol comparison in the primary study

key_findings.finding: The searches identified no primary study directly testing 7-dehydrocholesterol or a generic oxysterol in corneal endothelial or lens epithelial cells with apoptosis as the endpoint; the retrieved results were reviews or unrelated ocular studies. Therefore, evidence for 7-dehydrocholesterol/other oxysterols in these two cell types is insufficient, and their effects should not be conflated with the cholestanol result.
